content.text: The text reviews gastric ulcer, gastric cancer, hemorrhage, and gastric dilatation. Gastric ulcer may remain latent, follow a chronic course, heal with deforming scars, or cause fatal perforation, hemorrhage, abscesses, fistulas, peritonitis, and pyloric stenosis. Its causes remain uncertain, with circulatory injury and digestion by gastric juice prominent theories. Diagnosis relies on characteristic epigastric pain, vomiting, and hematemesis; treatment emphasizes rest, bland liquid nutrition, rectal feeding when necessary, symptom control, and cautious surgery for perforation or obstruction. Gastric cancer usually affects older adults, especially the pyloric region, producing anorexia, pain, vomiting, coffee-ground emesis, tumor, progressive wasting, anemia, cachexia, and metastases. It is generally fatal, though rare surgical resection may prolong life. Gastric dilatation results from pyloric obstruction, excessive or fermenting contents, or muscular weakness, causing delayed vomiting, retained food, fermentation, splashing sounds, and emaciation; treatment centers on dietary restriction and stomach-tube irrigation.
